title: New Grub Street: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: The Grub Street Trap: Gissing's Opening Gambit

utterances.text: Welcome to New Grub Street Unpacked — a close reading of George Gissing's great, bruising novel about what it costs to be a writer.
Published in 1891, New Grub Street is one of the most unsentimental portraits of literary life ever written — and one of the most prophetic.

Over this episode, we'll be tracing Gissing's opening gambit — how he sets his trap, introduces his doomed and not-quite-doomed characters, and makes the literary marketplace feel as inescapable as gravity.
I'm joined today by three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose fascination is with how fiction is architecturally built — how Gissing constructs his effects sentence by sentence.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what poverty looked like in the 1880s — and can tell us what it meant, practically and brutally, to be a writer without money.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read New Grub Street as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since — with fresh fury and fresh admiration each time.
Let's begin at the beginning — with Gissing's title, his premise, and the world he drops us into on the very first page.
What strikes me every time I return to the opening is how immediately Gissing establishes his two-world structure.
We have Edwin Reardon and Jasper Milvain introduced almost in the same breath — and they are essentially thesis and antithesis.
Reardon is the man who writes because he must — because there is something in him that demands expression, regardless of whether the market wants it.
Milvain, by contrast, announces himself in the very first chapter with what I think is one of the most startling opening declarations in Victorian fiction.
He says, quite cheerfully: "I am not in a position to live as a poor man."
That coolness is everything — Milvain has already decided that literature is a trade, and that sentiment about art is a luxury he cannot afford.
Gissing places that declaration in the first pages almost as a provocation — here is your villain, except he isn't quite a villain, which is the whole terrible point.
Eleanor is right that it's a provocation — and what makes it historically vertiginous is that Milvain is not wrong about the economics.
By the 1880s, the literary marketplace in London had become genuinely industrialised.
The three-volume novel — the famous three-decker — was still the dominant form, but it was already dying, sustained artificially by the circulating libraries like Mudie's.
And the moment Mudie's stopped subsidising the form — which happened, fatally, just two years after Gissing published this novel — the whole architecture collapsed.
Gissing was writing about a world he could see ending, and Milvain is the man who has read the signs correctly.
What Gissing captures so precisely is that Milvain doesn't celebrate this — he simply accepts it, which is in some ways more chilling.
I want to come in on that word "chilling," because I think Gissing does something quite extraordinary with Milvain that isn't always noticed.
He makes him likeable.
Milvain is charming, witty, clear-eyed — and when he talks about the literary world, he says what everyone privately knows but won't say aloud.

There's that early moment where he describes Reardon's situation with almost clinical sympathy — something to the effect that Reardon is a man who has no chance because he insists on writing what he believes in rather than what will sell.
And you find yourself nodding along with Milvain — and then you feel rather ashamed of yourself for doing so.
That is the trap Gissing springs on the reader in the very first chapters — he implicates you in the system before you've noticed it's happening.
That's beautifully put — and it connects to the structural choice Gissing makes with his narrator.
The narrative voice in New Grub Street is close third-person, but it moves — it slips between characters with extraordinary freedom.
In one scene we are inside Reardon's anguish, and then Gissing pulls back and lets Milvain's cool assessment re-frame everything we've just felt.
It's deeply destabilising — which is precisely the point.
Gissing won't let you settle into comfortable sympathy with any single character for very long.
There's also the matter of Gissing's own position, which I think is impossible to ignore when reading the opening chapters.
He was living in precisely the circumstances he describes — writing against deadlines, in poverty, in a failing marriage, watching the market grind down writers he admired.
And yet the novel is not a self-pitying document — which is remarkable.
Gissing puts his most persuasive arguments in the mouth of Milvain, the man who has sold out — or rather, has never bothered with illusions in the first place.
That is a kind of intellectual honesty that I find almost painful.
And the women — I have to bring in the women, because Gissing's portrait of Amy Reardon from the very first pages is doing so much work.
Amy is not a villain either, and she's not quite a victim — she is a woman of intelligence trapped in a situation where her options are bounded entirely by her husband's income.
Gissing gives her a clarity about money that matches Milvain's — and there's something almost sisterly in their shared pragmatism, though they barely inhabit the same scenes.
What I find devastating is that she married Reardon believing he would be successful — and that belief was not unreasonable.
He had had a success.
The trap was already closing before the novel begins.
That point about the trap closing before the novel begins is crucial to how Gissing structures his opening gambit.
We arrive in medias res, but not in the sense of action — we arrive in the middle of a slow catastrophe.
Reardon's creative failure is already underway; the marriage is already under strain; the money is already running short.
Gissing denies us even the consolation of watching someone fall — we join the fall already in progress.
A slow catastrophe already underway — and a cast of characters each navigating their own version of the Grub Street trap.

In our next segment, we'll follow Reardon deeper into that catastrophe — into the agony of the blank page, the crumbling marriage, and what Gissing makes of artistic failure as a subject worthy of a great novel.

segments.title: Reardon's Unravelling: Ambition, Failure, and the Writer's Fate

utterances.text: We've been looking at how Gissing sets his trap in those opening chapters — the literary marketplace laid bare, its machinery already grinding.
Now I want to turn to the man caught most completely in its teeth: Edwin Reardon.
His is the novel's most sustained study of a writer failing — not from lack of talent, but from something more painful than that.
What's so extraordinary about Reardon is that Gissing refuses to let him be simply a victim.
He has real gifts — we're told this, and we believe it — but he's constitutionally unable to produce under the conditions that the market demands.
There's a scene — and it haunts the whole novel — where Reardon sits before his manuscript and simply cannot write.
Not won't. Cannot.
Gissing describes him counting the words he's written — obsessively, pathetically — as if arithmetic might substitute for inspiration.
That image of a man measuring his failure by the word is one of the most devastating things in Victorian fiction.
And it's worth being precise about what Reardon is actually up against materially, because it's easy to aestheticise his suffering.
The three-volume novel — the triple-decker — was the dominant commercial form, and circulating libraries like Mudie's essentially set the terms of production.
You had to produce roughly three hundred pages per volume, which meant padding, which meant diluting whatever genuine vision you had.
Reardon knows this. He says it openly — that he's being asked to manufacture bulk rather than write a book.

Gissing captures the exact phrase Reardon uses about his situation — something to the effect that a man of his temperament simply cannot do it, that the demand is for quantity, and quantity kills him.
The structural injustice there is clear: the market has no mechanism for accommodating the writer who needs time and silence.
It rewards fluency and punishes depth. That is not an accident of this particular marketplace — it is its logic.
What moves me most, rereading Reardon's sections, is how Gissing tracks the exact stages of a creative person's disintegration.
First there's the anxiety — the sense that the next book might not come.
Then the forced production — grinding out pages he despises.
Then the collapse of faith in himself entirely.
There's a moment where he reflects that he once wrote because he had something to say, and now he writes because he must pay the rent.
And the terrible thing is that Amy — his wife — cannot pretend that this distinction doesn't matter.
She married someone she believed would rise. She watches him sink instead.
And Gissing is merciless about the fact that her disappointment is entirely reasonable.
Yes — and that's where Gissing's craft becomes almost uncomfortable to admire.
He gives Amy a completely coherent inner logic, so you cannot simply dismiss her as cold or mercenary.
She grew up expecting a certain material life; she made a gamble on Reardon's talent; the gamble is not paying off.
What Gissing does structurally — and this is the architecture I keep coming back to — is interleave Reardon's deterioration with Jasper Milvain's ascent.
Every chapter where Reardon fails to write a page, Milvain has dashed off a column, charmed an editor, positioned himself perfectly.
The juxtaposition is almost too neat — but Gissing earns it because both men are fully realised, not symbols.
There's a specific episode I want to put on the table: Reardon's decision to take the clerkship.
When he accepts a hospital clerk's position — essentially admitting defeat as a literary man — it's framed as a kind of social death.
And in Victorian terms, he's right to experience it that way. Class was enacted through occupation, through address, through the cut of your coat.
A gentleman who had published novels returning to clerical work was not merely changing jobs — he was changing caste.
Amy's departure — the separation — follows almost inevitably from this, not because she's unfeeling but because the social scaffolding of their marriage has collapsed.
Gissing understands that marriages are partly social contracts, and when the contract fails, the emotion alone cannot sustain the structure.
And yet — and this is what I keep returning to — there's a tenderness in how Gissing writes Reardon's final months.
Separated from Amy, living cheaply in Islington, he actually recovers something — a kind of quietness, an ability to read again for pleasure.
There's a passage where he reads Greek — just reads it, for himself, not for any project — and Gissing conveys this as a kind of grace.
He was always this person — the scholar, the genuine reader — and the literary marketplace had no use for that person at all.
His death, when it comes, doesn't feel like tragedy in the operatic sense. It feels like exhaustion.
A man who was worn down, not destroyed by a single blow.
That's beautifully put. And I think Gissing's own position as a writer shadows every page of Reardon's story.
This is autobiography transmuted into fiction — but transmuted carefully, with real artistic distance.
He doesn't sentimentalise Reardon. He doesn't excuse the self-pity, the occasional passive cruelty toward Amy.
What he does is something harder: he asks us to hold the full complexity of a man who is both genuinely gifted and genuinely unable to function.
That combination is what makes Reardon one of the great fictional portraits of the artist — not the romantic kind, the defeated kind.
The defeated artist — set against the artist who never allows himself to be defeated because he never quite believed in art in the first place.
Which brings us, of course, to Jasper Milvain — and the question of what it looks like when someone learns not to be Reardon.

segments.title: The Market Made Flesh: How Milvain Learns to Thrive

utterances.text: We've been sitting with Edwin Reardon's slow collapse — the man who cannot bend himself to the market's demands.
Now let's turn to the man who can — and does so with almost frightening ease.
Jasper Milvain: the novel's great pragmatist, its most uncomfortably recognisable figure, and perhaps its most brilliantly constructed character.
What Gissing does with Milvain is structurally audacious, I think.
He gives us a villain — because Milvain is, in functional terms, the antagonist — but he writes him with such lucid self-awareness that we can't dismiss him.
The very first chapter, Milvain sits at breakfast and announces, almost cheerfully, that he is the kind of man who will succeed precisely because he has no illusions.
He tells his sisters something to the effect that a man who wants to get on must study the market, not his own taste.
"Literature nowadays is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman."
And the chilling thing is that he says it without shame — almost with pride in his own clarity.
Gissing makes him the mouthpiece of a truth the novel would rather not be true.
That diagnosis of literature as trade was not rhetorical flourish in 1891 — it was economic fact.
The expansion of the periodical press, the circulating libraries, the three-volume novel system — all of it created a machinery that rewarded a particular kind of productivity.
Milvain understands that machinery with the instincts of an engineer rather than an artist.
And what strikes me historically is how modern his method is — networking, cultivating editors, making himself useful to people with influence.
His relationship with Clement Fadge, the powerful editor, is essentially a masterclass in literary careerism.
He courts the man's favour deliberately, systematically, without any pretence that he is doing otherwise.
What I find almost unbearable to read is how good Milvain is at it.
Because he's not simply cynical — he's charming, he's intelligent, and you can see why people open doors for him.
There's that passage where he reflects on his own strategy almost with aesthetic pleasure — as though planning his career were itself a creative act.
He says something like: he is not of the race who are ruined by their scruples.
And you feel Gissing writing that line with a kind of bitter admiration.
He hates what Milvain represents but he can see the world through Milvain's eyes with terrible vividness.
That split in Gissing's sympathy is what makes the novel so formally uncomfortable to inhabit.
The narration never simply condemns Milvain — it follows him too closely, renders his reasoning too faithfully.
And structurally, Gissing gives Milvain the success the novel's moral architecture perhaps ought to deny him.
He gets the career. He gets Amy. He gets the editorship.
Gissing refuses to write the redemptive ending where virtue triumphs — and that refusal is the novel's most radical gesture.
And yet I want to resist reading Milvain as purely a figure of moral failure.
He's honest — which in this world is more than can be said for several characters who hold themselves to higher standards.
He tells Marian — to her face, essentially — that he cannot afford to marry her while she is without money.
It's brutal, but it is a kind of honesty that the novel's more romantically inclined characters never manage.
Reardon, by contrast, enters marriage without the means to sustain it and destroys two lives in the process.
I take James's point — but I think that honesty costs Marian everything, and that's where my sympathy breaks.
He courts her, allows her to love him, and then withdraws when the inheritance disappears.
The scene where she realises what is happening — where she begins to read his letters differently — is some of the most quietly devastating writing in the novel.
And Milvain walks away clean. His career continues its upward arc.
That is where Gissing's naturalism becomes something almost savage.
And the craft of it is that we watch Milvain rationalise each step so plausibly that we almost agree with him in the moment.
Gissing is doing something very close to what we'd now call free indirect discourse — sliding into Milvain's perspective without fully endorsing it.
There's a moment when Milvain reflects that a man of his temperament must not allow feeling to obstruct calculation.
And Gissing renders that thought with such syntactic composure that we momentarily inhabit the logic rather than judge it.
That is the technique at its most insidious — and most brilliant.
There's a broader social point embedded there, though.
The literary world Gissing depicts has no mechanism for rewarding scruple — it rewards volume, visibility, and connection.
Milvain isn't morally exceptional — he has simply read the rules of the game more clearly than anyone else.
And when he tells his sisters early on that a man must make his name known, that the name itself becomes the commodity — that is not a private philosophy.
That is a description of the literary economy Gissing observed around him.
Replace the periodicals with social media and the editors with algorithms — the structure is identical.
That's the line that always stops me cold when I come back to the novel — the realisation that Gissing wasn't writing history.
He was writing prophecy.
Milvain is the figure the literary world now produces in abundance — people who are very good at being writers without necessarily being very good at writing.
And Gissing mourns this without quite being able to say that Reardon's way was better — because Reardon's way ends in misery and early death.
Milvain triumphant, Reardon destroyed — and caught between them, a woman whose story the novel has been quietly telling all along.
Marian Yule — the scholar in the British Museum Reading Room, the dutiful daughter, the discarded lover.
We'll turn to her story next — and to the question of what the novel sees when it looks at a woman of genuine intelligence trapped in this world.
We've been watching Jasper Milvain calculate his way through literary London — treating every relationship as a rung on a ladder.
But there's a figure at the centre of this novel whose relationship to literary work couldn't be more different — and whose story, I think, is the book's most devastating.
Marian Yule: scholar's daughter, library drudge, woman of genuine intellectual gifts — trapped between pages she did not choose.
Caroline, you've always had strong feelings about Marian — where do you want to begin?
Marian is the character I find myself defending most fiercely every time I re-read this novel.
Because Gissing gives her everything — intelligence, sensitivity, moral seriousness — and then systematically refuses to let any of it matter.
There's that extraordinary passage early on where she's working in the British Museum Reading Room, and Gissing describes the fog pressing against the dome.
"A word, a phrase, a sentence, of very ordinary import, would be pondered for a whole minute before it yielded its true meaning."
That's not just describing mental fatigue — it's describing a mind that has been worn smooth by work that asks nothing of it.
She is brilliant, and she is exhausted, and those two things are in constant terrible tension.
And what I find so architecturally bold about Gissing's treatment of Marian is precisely that contrast you're pointing to.
The Reading Room itself becomes a kind of character — or rather, a kind of argument made out of stone and fog.
Gissing describes it as a "gloomy and oppressive" space — and that's not incidental atmospheric dressing.
"The readers who sat here from ten to four, day after day, year after year — what could they produce but sterility?"
That's Marian's own thought — Gissing gives her the diagnostic clarity to see exactly what is being done to her.
She understands the machine and she is inside it and she cannot get out.
That combination — lucidity without agency — is one of the cruelest things Gissing ever invented.
I want to put some pressure on the word 'invented,' though — because for women in Marian's situation, that machine was entirely real.
The British Museum Reading Room in the 1880s was one of the very few spaces where an educated woman could work — could be seen to work — without immediate social scandal.
And yet the work itself — indexing, cross-referencing, doing the intellectual labour that sustains other men's books — was entirely invisible.
Marian's father, Alfred Yule, treats her quite literally as an extension of his own scholarly apparatus.
She reads for him, she notes for him, she structures arguments that will appear under his name.
That is not a fictional invention — that is a documentary record of how women's intellectual labour was absorbed and erased.
And the thing is, Marian doesn't rage against it — at least not openly.
Gissing is too honest a novelist to give her a scene of grand rebellion that the social structure would never have permitted.
Instead, her resistance is interior — and it comes through in these tiny, devastating flashes of self-awareness.
There's the moment she thinks about what it would mean to have money of her own — really her own — and Gissing writes it with such compressed longing.
"To have money — to be free — to go her own way, write her own books, live as her nature bade her."
Three clauses, three freedoms — and all three equally impossible.
The sentence structure itself performs the wish — and its foreclosure.
That is such a precise observation — because Gissing is doing something quite unusual for a male novelist of this period.
He's not merely sympathetic to Marian — he actually writes her interiority with full imaginative credibility.
The Jasper Milvain plot and the Marian plot run in counterpoint — and what Gissing understands is that they are playing the same game by different rules.
Jasper can treat people as instruments of ambition and be rewarded for it.
Marian is herself treated as an instrument — and when she reaches for something like what Jasper has, the inheritance, the chance at independence, it slips away.
The uncle's failed fortune isn't just a plot reversal — it's the novel saying: the game was always rigged against her.
And Jasper's behaviour when that inheritance disappears is, I think, the coldest thing in the novel.
He doesn't break with Marian dramatically — he simply withdraws, incrementally, until she understands.
It's the behaviour of a man who has absorbed market logic so completely that he cannot recognise it operating in his own emotional life.
And Gissing doesn't editorialize — he simply shows us Marian's face as she comprehends what is happening.
There's a kind of documentary restraint in those scenes that I find more damning than any authorial outrage could be.
What breaks my heart about Marian's ending is precisely that there is no catharsis.
She goes to Wattleborough — to a provincial librarian's post — and Gissing describes it without sentiment or rescue.
Her intellectual gifts find their level in a small-town library, and the novel closes on her without pity and without consolation.
That refusal of consolation is, I think, one of the most radical things about New Grub Street — it's a realist novel that takes realism absolutely seriously.
Most Victorian novels find a way to reward moral seriousness.
Gissing simply does not.
Marian's story makes the personal cost of literary culture visceral in a way that no argument could.

And that invites us to look more broadly at the social architecture that produced her situation — the class structures, the publishing economy, the whole machinery that determined who could write and who could only serve.
That's exactly what we'll be turning to next.

segments.title: Grub Street's Social Machine: Class, Commerce, and Literary Culture

utterances.text: We've been dwelling on Marian's predicament — her intellect caged by circumstance and by her father's ambitions.
But her story is really one thread in a much larger social fabric that Gissing is weaving.
This segment, we want to pull back and look at the whole machine — the economics, the class pressures, the publishing world — that grinds people like Marian and Edwin Reardon down.
The machine metaphor is apt, and I'd push it even further.

What Gissing is depicting with extraordinary precision is the commodification of literary labour in the 1880s — a moment when the three-volume novel was collapsing, the cheap periodical press was exploding, and writing had become, for the first time, something you could plausibly attempt to live by.
The cruelty is that it had become plausible — just plausible enough to trap people.
Reardon is not a fool and he is not without talent.
He simply cannot produce the volume of competent, marketable prose that the new literary economy demands, quickly enough, reliably enough, to survive.
And what's so devastating about Gissing's treatment is that he refuses to make it simply a tale of talent crushed by philistines.
The market isn't villainous in a cartoonish way — it's just indifferent.
And that indifference is far more frightening than malice would be.
Think about Jasper Milvain — Gissing gives us this wonderfully clear-eyed opportunist who understands the market completely and makes no apology for it.
He opens the novel almost as a manifesto — telling his sisters that the days of writing for posterity are over, that the craft is now about understanding what editors want this season.
Gissing sets Milvain and Reardon side by side as a kind of structural argument — not a moral one.
What strikes me every time I re-read the opening chapters is how Gissing deploys that contrast almost immediately — and how uncomfortable he makes you feel about where your sympathies land.
Because Milvain is genuinely charming.
He's witty, he's honest about his ambitions in a way that's almost refreshing.
And then Gissing gives him this line early on — something to the effect that he is not a man of genius, so he will be an editor, and a successful one.
"I have no strong moral convictions" — that's essentially Milvain's creed, delivered with complete cheerfulness.
And you can see why people find him refreshing — and also why Gissing wants you to notice that refreshingness is itself a kind of danger.
The class dimension here is one that I think readers sometimes underweight.
Milvain has a certain kind of social confidence — he knows how to move in drawing rooms, how to cultivate editors, how to make himself useful to people with power.
Reardon, crucially, does not have that confidence — and neither does he have the income that would purchase the time to write slowly and well.
There's a passage where Reardon reflects, quite bitterly, that poverty is not merely uncomfortable — it actively destroys the conditions under which serious thought is possible.

"The art of writing is the art of applying the seat of the trousers to the seat of the chair" — well, that's the old joke, but Gissing knows that without a chair in a warm room with a quiet hour, you simply cannot do it.
And Reardon has a wife who wants better rooms and a social position, which adds a particular kind of pressure that is historically very precise.
Amy is such a complex creation for that reason.
Gissing doesn't let you dismiss her as simply a cold, mercenary woman — which would be the easy thing, the Victorian-novel easy thing.
She married Reardon believing in him, and what erodes her belief is not greed — it's shame.
The shame of genteel poverty, of having to economise in ways that are visible to her social circle.
There's that devastating scene where the question of whether they can afford a second servant becomes almost a marital crisis.
Gissing is absolutely precise about how these small material humiliations accumulate into a catastrophe of feeling.
And the tragedy is that they're both right — that's what Gissing does that most novelists wouldn't dare.
Amy is right that their circumstances are genuinely degrading and that Reardon's paralysis is making things worse.
Reardon is right that the work he's being pressured to produce is not worth producing — that hack-work corrodes the mind that has to generate it.
He says something like — and this stays with me — that to write without believing in what you're writing is a kind of slow self-murder.
Gissing gives that weight — he doesn't soften it or make Reardon melodramatic.
It reads as a clinical observation, which makes it worse.
The figure of Whelpdale is worth introducing here as a kind of comic counterpoint to all of this — though a rather rueful comedy.
Whelpdale is the man who fails at everything literary and then invents a new kind of penny weekly — Chit-Chat, he calls it — aimed at readers who can't concentrate for more than a few hundred words.
And the thing is — he succeeds.
Gissing has him explain with complete seriousness that the publication will never contain anything that taxes the reader, that the sentences will be short, the paragraphs shorter.
It is a perfect satirical description of a certain kind of content optimisation that feels absolutely contemporary.
One hundred and thirty years ago, and Gissing had diagnosed it precisely.
Chit-Chat is genuinely one of the funniest and bleakest inventions in the novel.
Because Whelpdale isn't cynical about it — he's enthusiastic.
He genuinely believes he's found a democratic gap in the market — reaching readers who were previously unreached.
And Gissing doesn't quite let you laugh at Whelpdale without also implicating you in the question of what culture is actually for.
Is literary culture a preserve for those with sufficient leisure to appreciate difficulty?
Or does Whelpdale have a point?
I think what gives the novel its particular ache is that Gissing himself is implicated in all of this.
He was writing it under exactly the conditions he describes — under financial pressure, producing more than he wished, faster than felt right.
And yet it's a remarkably controlled, architecturally precise book — which is itself a kind of argument against the system that produced it.
Reardon at one point talks about the conditions the Greeks wrote under — having time, having the culture that valued their efforts, having an audience that was also their community.
And it sounds nostalgic and self-pitying on the surface, but Gissing frames it so you feel the genuine loss.
The loss of a world in which the serious writer and the society could still speak the same language.
And Gissing never lets that loss tip into simple romanticism — which is what keeps this novel so tightly coiled.
The social machine grinds, but Gissing also sees the absurdity of it — and in our next segment, we're going to look at precisely that.
The dark comedy in New Grub Street — the scenes where the desperation becomes, if not quite funny, then savagely, recognisably comic.

segments.title: The Comedy of Desperation: Gissing's Satirical Eye

utterances.text: We've been mapping the social machinery of Gissing's world — the economics, the class pressures, the brutal arithmetic of literary survival.
But there's another dimension to New Grub Street that I think we sometimes underplay — the fact that it is, at moments, savagely funny.
Eleanor, I want to start with you on this — where does the comedy live in this novel, and what is Gissing doing with it?
It's a comedy of total incongruity — and that's the most precise way I can put it.
You have characters of genuine literary sensitivity — real aesthetic feeling — trapped inside a system that treats words as so many yards of cheap cloth.
The gap between their self-conception and their actual circumstances is the engine of the satire.
Think of Jasper Milvain at the very opening of the novel, cheerfully calculating the commercial value of a recently deceased author before the man is cold.
He says something to the effect that the man's death is excellent timing — it'll make his biography sell.
And Gissing gives him that line with absolutely no authorial flinch — no wink, no condemnation in the prose itself.
That deadpan quality is where the comedy cuts deepest.
And Milvain is consistently funny precisely because he is so completely right about how the world works.
His cynicism isn't a pose — it's an accurate reading of the literary marketplace of the 1880s.
The comedy comes from the fact that the character who is most morally repugnant is also the character giving the audience the most reliable economic commentary.
He tells his sister Dora quite early on that one must write for the market, not for posterity — and the novel proves him correct at every turn.
There's a particular dry comedy in the scenes where he's coaching the Milvain sisters in how to produce marketable hackwork — treating literature as a skill set to be acquired, like bookkeeping.
Gissing clearly finds this grotesque — and yet the prose never lets us feel entirely superior to Jasper.
What gets me is the comedy around Reardon's pride — the way his literary dignity keeps colliding with absolute material desperation.
There's a scene I always return to — where Reardon is trying to write and has to count how many words he's produced in an evening.
He's reduced to measuring his creative output like a factory worker measuring output — words per hour, almost.
And Gissing gives us Reardon's internal anguish about this with complete seriousness — but the structural joke is inescapable.
The man who writes about the human soul is calculating whether he can afford to write about the human soul this week.
It's genuinely painful — and yet you catch yourself almost laughing, which makes it more painful.
That double response is Gissing's signature — he wants you to feel both reactions simultaneously, and he engineers it with real craft.
Think about Alfred Yule — who is perhaps the funniest character in the novel in the most desolating way.
Here is a man of genuine learning, genuine literary judgment, who has been ground down by decades of reviewing and hack editing into something almost feral in his bitterness.
His relationship with his wife is a sustained comedy of social embarrassment — she is uneducated, she drops her aitches, she represents everything he despises about his own origins.
And he married her when he was poor, and now he can't forgive her for being the witness to that poverty.

The comedy is in the specificity — Gissing renders the dinner-table silences, the pointed corrections, the accumulated cruelties of a literary man who turns his critical faculties on his own household.
Yule is a portrait of what happens to a man when resentment becomes the organising principle of a life.
And the satire is historically precise — the literary reviewing culture of the period really did create these figures.
Men who had spent thirty years writing unsigned reviews for periodicals that paid almost nothing, accumulating knowledge that no one valued in the form in which they possessed it.
There's a magnificently bleak comedy in the subplot about the literary journal Yule dreams of editing — his one ambition, the thing that might redeem the years of drudgery.
And of course the money doesn't materialise, and the opportunity collapses, and he goes blind.
Gissing does not spare anyone — but there is something almost Dickensian in the extravagance of Yule's particular fate.
I want to talk about Whelpdale — because I think he's the character Gissing allows himself to be genuinely fond of, even while he's satirising him.
He's the eternal optimist of literary failure — forever launching schemes, forever cheerful about his latest disaster.
He's the one who eventually launches that magazine — Chat, I think it's called — aimed at readers with a ten-minute attention span.
And the joke is that it succeeds — of course it succeeds, because it's perfectly calibrated to what the market actually wants.
Whelpdale figures out, almost accidentally, what Jasper knows by cold calculation — that the reading public does not want what Reardon is offering.
And yet you like Whelpdale — which means the comedy doesn't curdle into contempt the way it might with a lesser satirist.
That's the crucial distinction — between satire that annihilates its subjects and satire that understands them.
Gissing is, I think, fundamentally a novelist of sympathy even when he is at his most satirical.
Even Jasper — who is the closest thing to a villain — is given the dignity of internal consistency.
His choices are comprehensible — that's what makes the comedy uncomfortable rather than reassuring.
We laugh at Jasper's calculation, but we can't entirely dismiss the calculation — because Gissing has shown us the world that makes it rational.
There's also the comedy of the novel's women navigating this world — which I don't think gets discussed enough.
Amy Reardon's predicament is structurally comic in the darkest possible way — she married a man she believed was ascending, and she is watching him descend in real time.
She has genuine intelligence and genuine social ambition, and the only instrument available to her is her husband's pen — which is failing.
The scenes of their marital deterioration have a bleak comedy of mismatched timing — each one trying to have a different conversation than the other.
Reardon wants to discuss his artistic soul; Amy needs to discuss the rent.
And there's something almost farcical about the speed with which Amy pivots to Milvain once Reardon is dead — almost indecently fast.
Gissing doesn't editorialize — he just gives us the timeline, and the timeline is the joke.
And yet — and this is the thing that stops it from being mere satirical cruelty — you understand Amy completely.
She is making the rational choice, the survivable choice, in a world that offers her no other instruments.
The comedy and the tragedy are the same thing — which is, I think, where Gissing is at his most genuinely modern.
That phrase — the comedy and the tragedy are the same thing — feels like an ideal hinge into what I want to explore next.
Because when we look at how Gissing resolves — or refuses to resolve — these characters' fates, the question of what the novel's final note actually is becomes urgent and difficult.
That's where we're heading next — no exit, and the tragedy of compromise.

segments.title: No Exit: Synthesis and the Tragedy of Compromise

utterances.text: That satirical edge we've been tracing — the comedy of desperation — never quite lets you forget the tragedy underneath it.
And in this final segment, I want us to sit with what the novel ultimately argues — about compromise, about survival, and about what gets lost in both.
What strikes me most, returning to the novel as a whole, is how ruthlessly Gissing structures it as a series of closed doors.
Reardon can't write commercially without killing something in himself, and he can't write artistically without starving his family.
There is genuinely no exit that doesn't cost him everything.
And Gissing makes that architectural — it's built into the novel's bones, not arrived at sentimentally.
There's a moment near the end where Reardon reflects on what he might have been, and Gissing gives it to us in free indirect style — so we feel the grief from the inside.
"He had capacities which, under different circumstances, might have made him a considerable man."
That word 'capacities' is devastating — it's so precise and so cold, like a coroner's verdict.
And what makes Reardon's situation so historically accurate is that the market really did work exactly that way in the 1880s.
The three-volume novel was collapsing as a commercial form, the circulating libraries were dictating length and content, and literary journalism paid almost nothing.
Reardon isn't simply unlucky — he's caught in a structural transformation of the literary economy.
Which is what gives Jasper Milvain his peculiar moral charge in the novel.
Milvain isn't a villain — he simply reads the market correctly and adjusts himself to it without self-deception.
He says as much at the very opening of the novel — I'm a man of my time, he tells his sisters, literature is a trade.
"Literature nowadays is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic accident, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman."
Gissing puts the whole thesis of the novel into Milvain's mouth on page one, and has the nerve to let him be right.
What I find hardest to shake is Amy.
Because readers often judge her — she leaves Reardon, she eventually marries Milvain — and I think that judgment is exactly the trap Gissing is setting.
She is also a person with no good options, living in a world that gives women even fewer exits than it gives men.
There's that terrible scene when she goes back to her mother's and Reardon comes to visit, and you can feel the love that's still there — and the absolute impossibility of it.
Gissing doesn't sentimentalise it.
He gives us Amy thinking, in her clear, cold way, that poverty has done this — not lack of feeling, but poverty.
"Poverty degrades, and deforms, and corrupts. No human being can retain dignity under its persistent pressure."
She's right. That's the unbearable thing — she is simply right.
And Biffen is the figure Gissing uses to take that argument to its absolute extreme.
Reardon at least has a marriage, a child, some vestige of social connection.
Biffen has nothing but his art — his insane, heroic, completely unmarketable project of absolute realism.
He wants to write a novel about a man called Mr. Bailey, a grocer — utterly ordinary, utterly true, utterly unpublishable.
And when Biffen finally finishes it and it fails completely, Gissing gives him a death that is almost serene.
"He had always been a poor, struggling, obscure man; he would die as he had lived."
There's no bitterness in that line — just an awful clarity, which is somehow worse.
The contrast with Milvain's ending is almost too stark to be accidental.
Milvain marries Amy, inherits through her, edits his successful journal — everything works out for him, by every material measure.
And Gissing doesn't punish him for it.
There's no last-chapter revelation that Milvain secretly suffers or regrets his choices.
That refusal of conventional moral justice is, I think, the most radical thing Gissing does in the entire novel.
It is a novel without a providential ending — which in 1891 was a genuinely confrontational act.
And yet I always find myself going back to that final image of Marian Yule.
She loses Milvain, she loses the inheritance she'd hoped for, she ends up in some provincial post office job.

And she'd had that extraordinary chapter in the Reading Room of the British Museum — the fog pressing at the dome, the scholars grinding away, the sense of knowledge as a trap as much as a liberation.
Gissing writes her there as someone who sees through the whole machinery of literary production — and then has nowhere to go with that vision.
She's perhaps the most modern figure in the book — a woman with genuine intellectual gifts and absolutely no infrastructure to support them.
And she just — disappears from the novel, quietly, without ceremony.
That's the formal correlative of everything the novel argues, isn't it.
The people who deserve the most — Reardon, Biffen, Marian — are the ones the narrative itself can barely hold onto.
They slip away. The market absorbs the Milvains and discards the rest.
And the novel's structure enacts that — it doesn't fight it, it demonstrates it with a kind of terrible fidelity.
I think that phrase — terrible fidelity — might be the best description of what Gissing achieves in this novel that I've heard.
He doesn't spare us, and he doesn't spare his characters, and somehow that becomes a form of respect — for them, and for us as readers.

We've ranged widely today — through the machinery of literary commerce, the comedy and the cruelty of Gissing's satirical world, and now into the heart of what this novel is really asking us to sit with.
My deepest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, whose eye for the architecture of fiction has made passages I thought I knew feel completely new.
To James Blackstone, who has reminded us that behind every fictional hardship there are real institutions, real economies, and real people who suffered them.
And to Caroline Woodcourt, who has read this novel with the kind of loving attention it has always deserved and rarely received.
If you haven't read New Grub Street, I hope today has sent you straight to it.
If you have — well, I suspect you may want to read it again.
Thank you for listening.

‘The day before yesterday she went to Birmingham to see her father and

      kind of thing; they sell splendidly. Of course I shall make it a good
      advertisement of my business. Then I have a splendid idea. I’m going to
      advertise: “Novel-writing taught in ten lessons!” What do you think of
      that? No swindle; not a bit of it. I am quite capable of giving the
      ordinary man or woman ten very useful lessons. I’ve been working out the
      scheme; it would amuse you vastly, Reardon. The first lesson deals with
      the question of subjects, local colour—that kind of thing. I gravely
      advise people, if they possibly can, to write of the wealthy middle class;
      that’s the popular subject, you know. Lords and ladies are all very well,
      but the real thing to take is a story about people who have no titles, but
      live in good Philistine style. I urge study of horsey matters especially;
      that’s very important. You must be well up, too, in military grades, know
      about Sandhurst, and so on. Boating is an important topic. You see? Oh, I
      shall make a great thing of this. I shall teach my wife carefully, and
      then let her advertise lessons to girls; they’ll prefer coming to a woman,
      you know.’

c1:p43.text:
‘To be sure! To be sure!’ exclaimed their brother. ‘You have no faith. But
      just understand the difference between a man like Reardon and a man like
      me. He is the old type of unpractical artist; I am the literary man of
      1882. He won’t make concessions, or rather, he can’t make them; he can’t
      supply the market. I—well, you may say that at present I do nothing;
      but that’s a great mistake, I am learning my business. Literature nowadays
      is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic
      force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman. He thinks
      first and foremost of the markets; when one kind of goods begins to go off
      slackly, he is ready with something new and appetising. He knows perfectly
      all the possible sources of income. Whatever he has to sell he’ll get
      payment for it from all sorts of various quarters; none of your
      unpractical selling for a lump sum to a middleman who will make six
      distinct profits. Now, look you: if I had been in Reardon’s place, I’d
      have made four hundred at least out of “The Optimist”; I should have gone
      shrewdly to work with magazines and newspapers and foreign publishers, and—all
      sorts of people. Reardon can’t do that kind of thing, he’s behind his age;
      he sells a manuscript as if he lived in Sam Johnson’s Grub Street. But our
      Grub Street of to-day is quite a different place: it is supplied with
      telegraphic communication, it knows what literary fare is in demand in
      every part of the world, its inhabitants are men of business, however
      seedy.’
c1:p43.summary: Jasper articulates his philosophy: literature is a business, not an art; successful writers are those who understand the market and supply it strategically. He contrasts Reardon's 'old' unpractical approach with his own 'new' commercial method, emphasizing that writers must exploit all sources of income, manipulate magazines and newspapers, and treat their work as marketable goods rather than selling manuscripts for a lump sum like Samuel Johnson's era.
c1:p43.best_quote: Literature nowadays is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman.

c31:p4.text:
He worked very slowly. The book would make perhaps two volumes of ordinary
      novel size, but he had laboured over it for many months, patiently,
      affectionately, scrupulously. Each sentence was as good as he could make
      it, harmonious to the ear, with words of precious meaning skilfully set.
      Before sitting down to a chapter he planned it minutely in his mind; then
      he wrote a rough draft of it; then he elaborated the thing phrase by
      phrase. He had no thought of whether such toil would be recompensed in
      coin of the realm; nay, it was his conviction that, if with difficulty
      published, it could scarcely bring him money. The work must be
      significant, that was all he cared for. And he had no society of admiring
      friends to encourage him. Reardon understood the merit of the workmanship,
      but frankly owned that the book was repulsive to him. To the public it
      would be worse than repulsive—tedious, utterly uninteresting. No
      matter; it drew to its end.
c31:p4.summary: Biffen labours meticulously over 'Mr Bailey, Grocer,' planning and revising obsessively, knowing it will likely never earn him money or readers.

matched_quotes.text: A word, a phrase, a sentence, of very ordinary import, would be pondered for a whole minute before it yielded its true meaning.

c8:p19.text:
The fog grew thicker; she looked up at the windows beneath the dome and
      saw that they were a dusky yellow. Then her eye discerned an official
      walking along the upper gallery, and in pursuance of her grotesque humour,
      her mocking misery, she likened him to a black, lost soul, doomed to
      wander in an eternity of vain research along endless shelves. Or again,
      the readers who sat here at these radiating lines of desks, what were they
      but hapless flies caught in a huge web, its nucleus the great circle of
      the Catalogue? Darker, darker. From the towering wall of volumes seemed to
      emanate visible motes, intensifying the obscurity; in a moment the
      book-lined circumference of the room would be but a featureless
      prison-limit.

c15:p59.text:
‘I have thought of something, dearest. Do as you proposed last year; find
      a tenant for the flat whilst we still have a little money, and then go
      away into some quiet country place, where you can get back your health and
      live for very little, and write another book—a good book, that’ll
      bring you reputation again. I and Willie can go and live at mother’s for
      the summer months. Do this! It would cost you so little, living alone,
      wouldn’t it? You would know that I was well cared for; mother would be
      willing to have me for a few months, and it’s easy to explain that your

c12:p2.text:
In the time of waiting for the publishers’ offer, and now again when he
      was asking himself how he should use the respite granted him, Reardon
      spent his days at the British Museum. He could not read to much purpose,
      but it was better to sit here among strangers than seem to be idling under
      Amy’s glance. Sick of imaginative writing, he turned to the studies which
      had always been most congenial, and tried to shape out a paper or two like
      those he had formerly disposed of to editors. Among his unused material
      lay a mass of notes he had made in a reading of Diogenes Laertius, and it
      seemed to him now that he might make something salable out of these
      anecdotes of the philosophers. In a happier mood he could have written
      delightfully on such a subject—not learnedly, but in the strain of a
      modern man whose humour and sensibility find free play among the classic
      ghosts; even now he was able to recover something of the light touch which
      had given value to his published essays.
c12:p2.summary: Reardon spends his days at the British Museum, attempting to write scholarly essays on classical subjects based on his notes on Diogenes Laertius, partly to avoid appearing idle before Amy.

‘True. Can I think of a single subject in all the sphere of my experience
      without the consciousness that I see it through the medium of poverty? I
      have no enjoyment which isn’t tainted by that thought, and I can suffer no
      pain which it doesn’t increase. The curse of poverty is to the modern
      world just what that of slavery was to the ancient. Rich and destitute
      stand to each other as free man and bond. You remember the line of Homer I

c8:p0.text:
Of the acquaintances Yule had retained from his earlier years several were
      in the well-defined category of men with unpresentable wives. There was
      Hinks, for instance, whom, though in anger he spoke of him as a bore,
      Alfred held in some genuine regard. Hinks made perhaps a hundred a year
      out of a kind of writing which only certain publishers can get rid of and
      of this income he spent about a third on books. His wife was the daughter
      of a laundress, in whose house he had lodged thirty years ago, when new to
      London but already long-acquainted with hunger; they lived in complete
      harmony, but Mrs Hinks, who was four years the elder, still spoke the
      laundress tongue, unmitigated and immitigable. Another pair were Mr and
      Mrs Gorbutt. In this case there were no narrow circumstances to contend
      with, for the wife, originally a nursemaid, not long after her marriage
      inherited house property from a relative. Mr Gorbutt deemed himself a
      poet; since his accession to an income he had published, at his own
      expense, a yearly volume of verses; the only result being to keep alive
      rancour in his wife, who was both parsimonious and vain. Making no secret
      of it, Mrs Gorbutt rued the day on which she had wedded a man of letters,
      when by waiting so short a time she would have been enabled to aim at a
      prosperous tradesman, who kept his gig and had everything handsome about
      him. Mrs Yule suspected, not without reason, that this lady had an
      inclination to strong liquors. Thirdly came Mr and Mrs Christopherson, who
      were poor as church mice. Even in a friend’s house they wrangled
      incessantly, and made tragi-comical revelations of their home life. The
      husband worked casually at irresponsible journalism, but his chosen study
      was metaphysics; for many years he had had a huge and profound book on
      hand, which he believed would bring him fame, though he was not so
      unsettled in mind as to hope for anything else. When an article or two had
      earned enough money for immediate necessities he went off to the British
      Museum, and then the difficulty was to recall him to profitable exertions.
      Yet husband and wife had an affection for each other. Mrs Christopherson
      came from Camberwell, where her father, once upon a time, was the smallest
      of small butchers. Disagreeable stories were whispered concerning her
      earlier life, and probably the metaphysician did not care to look back in
      that direction. They had had three children; all were happily buried.
c8:p0.summary: Yule maintains friendships with several literary men whose marriages to women of lower social status have hindered their careers—Hinks married a laundress's daughter, Gorbutt a former nursemaid, and Christopherson a woman with a dubious past.
c8:p0.best_quote: There was Hinks, for instance, whom, though in anger he spoke of him as a bore, Alfred held in some genuine regard.

matched_quotes.text: He had always been a poor, struggling, obscure man; he would die as he had lived.

c31:p98.text:
I should have lived an intelligible life, instead of only trying to live,
      aiming at modes of life beyond my reach. My mistake was that of numberless
      men nowadays. Because I was conscious of brains, I thought that the only
      place for me was London. It’s easy enough to understand this common
      delusion. We form our ideas of London from old literature; we think of
      London as if it were still the one centre of intellectual life; we think
      and talk like Chatterton. But the truth is that intellectual men in our
      day do their best to keep away from London—when once they know the
      place. There are libraries everywhere; papers and magazines reach the
      north of Scotland as soon as they reach Brompton; it’s only on rare
      occasions, for special kinds of work, that one is bound to live in London.
      And as for recreation, why, now that no English theatre exists, what is
      there in London that you can’t enjoy in almost any part of England? At all
      events, a yearly visit of a week would be quite sufficient for all the
      special features of the town. London is only a huge shop, with an hotel on
      the upper storeys. To be sure, if you make it your artistic subject,
      that’s a different thing. But neither you nor I would do that by
      deliberate choice.’
c31:p98.summary: Reardon argues that London is a false magnet for ambitious writers, that intellectual life is available everywhere, and that London ruins artistic men.
c31:p98.best_quote: London is only a huge shop, with an hotel on the upper storeys.

c20:p48.text:
‘My husband is afraid Mr Reardon may fall seriously ill,’ said Mrs Carter.
      ‘And how dreadful! In such a place as that!’
c20:p48.summary: Jasper encounters Reardon on the street near the Yule house. Reardon's gaunt appearance and strange demeanor immediately concern him.

c10:p119.text:
‘I have thought of a new way of putting it. What I really aim at is an
      absolute realism in the sphere of the ignobly decent. The field, as I
      understand it, is a new one; I don’t know any writer who has treated
      ordinary vulgar life with fidelity and seriousness. Zola writes deliberate
      tragedies; his vilest figures become heroic from the place they fill in a
      strongly imagined drama. I want to deal with the essentially unheroic,
      with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the
      mercy of paltry circumstance. Dickens understood the possibility of such
      work, but his tendency to melodrama on the one hand, and his humour on the
      other, prevented him from thinking of it. An instance, now. As I came
      along by Regent’s Park half an hour ago a man and a girl were walking
      close in front of me, love-making; I passed them slowly and heard a good
      deal of their talk—it was part of the situation that they should pay
      no heed to a stranger’s proximity. Now, such a love-scene as that has
      absolutely never been written down; it was entirely decent, yet vulgar to
      the nth power. Dickens would have made it ludicrous—a gross
      injustice. Other men who deal with low-class life would perhaps have
      preferred idealising it—an absurdity. For my own part, I am going to
      reproduce it verbatim, without one single impertinent suggestion of any
      point of view save that of honest reporting. The result will be something
      unutterably tedious. Precisely. That is the stamp of the ignobly decent
      life. If it were anything but tedious it would be untrue. I speak, of
      course, of its effect upon the ordinary reader.’
c10:p119.summary: Biffen expounds his theory of absolute realism applied to ordinary, vulgar life—rejecting both Zola's melodrama and Dickens's humor, insisting instead on verbatim reproduction of the tedious, unheroic reality of common people.
c10:p119.best_quote: I want to deal with the essentially unheroic, with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the mercy of paltry circumstance

c17:p109.text:
‘And a grievous share of the fault lies with you, Amy. You remember very
      well when I first saw how dark the future was. I was driven even to say
      that we ought to change our mode of living; I asked you if you would be
      willing to leave this place and go into cheaper rooms. And you know what
      your answer was. Not a sign in you that you would stand by me if the worst
      came. I knew then what I had to look forward to, but I durst not believe
      it. I kept saying to myself: “She loves me, and as soon as she really
      understands—” That was all self-deception. If I had been a wise man,
      I should have spoken to you in a way you couldn’t mistake. I should have
      told you that we were living recklessly, and that I had determined to
      alter it. I have no delicacy? No regard for your feelings? Oh, if I had
      had less! I doubt whether you can even understand some of the
      considerations that weighed with me, and made me cowardly—though I
      once thought there was no refinement of sensibility that you couldn’t
      enter into. Yes, I was absurd enough to say to myself: “It will look as if
      I had consciously deceived her; she may suffer from the thought that I won
      her at all hazards, knowing that I should soon expose her to poverty and
      all sorts of humiliation.” Impossible to speak of that again; I had to
      struggle desperately on, trying to hope. Oh! if you knew—’
c17:p109.summary: Reardon argues Amy failed to support him in his crisis and that his delicacy prevented him from honestly telling her their situation was hopeless. He expresses his bitter recognition that her nature makes her unable to endure poverty.
c17:p109.best_quote: Yes, I was absurd enough to say to myself: 'It will look as if I had consciously deceived her; she may suffer from the thought that I won her at all hazards, knowing that I should soon expose her to poverty and all sorts of humiliation.' Impossible to speak of that again; I had to struggle desperately on, trying to hope.

c2:p77.text:
‘Civilisation!’ exclaimed John, scornfully. ‘What do you mean by
      civilisation? Do you call it civilising men to make them weak, flabby
      creatures, with ruined eyes and dyspeptic stomachs? Who is it that reads
      most of the stuff that’s poured out daily by the ton from the
      printing-press? Just the men and women who ought to spend their leisure
      hours in open-air exercise; the people who earn their bread by sedentary
      pursuits, and who need to live as soon as they are free from the desk or
      the counter, not to moon over small print. Your Board schools, your
      popular press, your spread of education! Machinery for ruining the
      country, that’s what I call it.’
c2:p77.summary: John launches into a scornful denunciation of civilization as weakening people through reading and sedentary pursuits; he attacks Board schools, popular press, and education as ruining England by making people pale, weak, and dyspeptic instead of promoting physical vigor and outdoor life.
c2:p77.best_quote: Your Board schools, your popular press, your spread of education! Machinery for ruining the country, that's what I call it.

c3:p121.text:
‘... The evil of the time is the multiplication of ephemerides. Hence a
      demand for essays, descriptive articles, fragments of criticism, out of
      all proportion to the supply of even tolerable work. The men who have an
      aptitude for turning out this kind of thing in vast quantities are
      enlisted by every new periodical, with the result that their productions
      are ultimately watered down into worthlessness.... Well now, there’s
      Fadge. Years ago some of Fadge’s work was not without a certain—a
      certain conditional promise of—of comparative merit; but now his
      writing, in my opinion, is altogether beneath consideration; how Rackett
      could be so benighted as to give him The Study—especially after a
      man like Henry Hawkridge—passes my comprehension. Did you read a
      paper of his, a few months back, in The Wayside, a preposterous
      rehabilitation of Elkanah Settle? Ha! Ha! That’s what such men are driven
      to. Elkanah Settle! And he hadn’t even a competent acquaintance with his
      paltry subject. Will you credit that he twice or thrice referred to
      Settle’s reply to “Absalom and Achitophel” by the title of “Absalom
      Transposed,” when every schoolgirl knows that the thing was called
      “Achitophel Transposed”! This was monstrous enough, but there was
      something still more contemptible. He positively, I assure you, attributed
      the play of “Epsom Wells” to Crowne! I should have presumed that every
      student of even the most trivial primer of literature was aware that
      “Epsom Wells” was written by Shadwell.... Now, if one were to take
      Shadwell for the subject of a paper, one might very well show how unjustly
      his name has fallen into contempt. It has often occurred to me to do this.
      “But Shadwell never deviates into sense.” The sneer, in my opinion, is
      entirely unmerited. For my own part, I put Shadwell very high among the
      dramatists of his time, and I think I could show that his absolute worth
      is by no means inconsiderable. Shadwell has distinct vigour of dramatic
      conception; his dialogue....’
c3:p121.summary: Alfred launches into a passionate critique of modern literary journalism: too many periodicals demand mediocre content; Fadge exemplifies declining standards through scholarly errors; yet Shadwell deserves reconsideration as a neglected dramatist.
c3:p121.best_quote: The evil of the time is the multiplication of ephemerides. Hence a demand for essays, descriptive articles, fragments of criticism, out of all proportion to the supply of even tolerable work.

c13:p2.text:
The May number of The Current, in its article headed ‘Books of the Month,’
      devoted about half a page to ‘English Prose in the Nineteenth Century.’
      This notice was a consummate example of the flippant style of attack.
      Flippancy, the most hopeless form of intellectual vice, was a
      characterising note of Mr Fadge’s periodical; his monthly comments on
      publications were already looked for with eagerness by that growing class
      of readers who care for nothing but what can be made matter of ridicule.
      The hostility of other reviewers was awkward and ineffectual compared with
      this venomous banter, which entertained by showing that in the book under
      notice there was neither entertainment nor any other kind of interest. To
      assail an author without increasing the number of his readers is the
      perfection of journalistic skill, and The Current, had it stood alone,
      would fully have achieved this end. As it was, silence might have been
      better tactics. But Mr Fadge knew that his enemy would smart under the
      poisoned pin-points, and that was something gained.
c13:p2.summary: The Current's review of Yule's book exemplifies the flippancy and venomous banter characteristic of Fadge's editorial approach, designed to entertain readers who seek only ridicule rather than genuine literary criticism.
c13:p2.best_quote: To assail an author without increasing the number of his readers is the perfection of journalistic skill

c16:p92.text:
He tore open the envelope. In delicacy Reardon and Biffen averted their
      eyes. There was silence for a minute, then a strange ejaculation from
      Whelpdale caused his friends to look up at him. He had gone pale, and was
      frowning at the sheet of paper which trembled in his hand.
c16:p92.summary: Whelpdale turns pale and trembles while reading the letter, his joy transformed instantly into shock and dismay.
c16:p92.best_quote: He had gone pale, and was frowning at the sheet of paper which trembled in his hand.

c16:p97.text:
‘She writes—that she has met an old lover—in Birmingham—that
      it was with him she had quarrelled-not with her father at all—that
      she ran away to annoy him and frighten him—that she has made it up
      again, and they’re going to be married!’
c16:p97.summary: Whelpdale reveals that his fiancée's letter explains she has reunited with an old lover in Birmingham and will marry him instead.
c16:p97.best_quote: She writes—that she has met an old lover—in Birmingham—that it was with him she had quarrelled-not with her father at all—that she ran away to annoy him and frighten him—that she has made it up again, and they're going to be married!

c22:p156.text:
‘I haven’t much faith in marrying for love, as you know. What’s more, I
      believe it’s the very rarest thing for people to be in love with each
      other. Reardon and his wife perhaps were an instance; perhaps—I’m
      not quite sure about her. As a rule, marriage is the result of a mild
      preference, encouraged by circumstances, and deliberately heightened into
      strong sexual feeling. You, of all men, know well enough that the same
      kind of feeling could be produced for almost any woman who wasn’t
      repulsive.’
c22:p156.summary: Jasper expounds his theory: genuine love is exceedingly rare; most marriages begin with mild preference that circumstances amplify into sexual attraction; the same feelings could be generated toward almost any acceptable woman.
c22:p156.best_quote: I haven't much faith in marrying for love, as you know. What's more, I believe it's the very rarest thing for people to be in love with each other. Reardon and his wife perhaps were an instance; perhaps—I'm not quite sure about her. As a rule, marriage is the result of a mild preference, encouraged by circumstances, and deliberately heightened into strong sexual feeling. You, of all men, know well enough that the same kind of feeling could be produced for almost any woman who wasn't repulsive.

c14:p155.text:
It was within his reach to marry a woman who would bring him wealth. He
      had that in mind; she understood it too well. But not one moment’s
      advantage would she relinquish. He must choose her in her poverty, and be
      content with what his talents could earn for him. Her love gave her the
      right to demand this sacrifice; let him ask for her love, and the
      sacrifice would no longer seem one, so passionately would she reward him.
c14:p155.summary: Marian insists that Jasper must choose her despite her lack of wealth, and that her love will compensate for any economic sacrifice. She believes her passion gives her the right to make this demand.
c14:p155.best_quote: He must choose her in her poverty, and be content with what his talents could earn for him. Her love gave her the right to demand this sacrifice; let him ask for her love, and the sacrifice would no longer seem one, so passionately would she reward him.

c15:p93.text:
‘Darling, they do struggle. But it’s as if an ever-increasing weight were
      round their necks; it drags them lower and lower. The world has no pity on
      a man who can’t do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be
      a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn’t take pity on you you will
      starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate. I have no
      right to complain of my own ill-fortune; it’s my own fault (in a sense)
      that I can’t continue as well as I began; if I could write books as good
      as the early ones I should earn money. For all that, it’s hard that I must
      be kicked aside as worthless just because I don’t know a trade.’
c15:p93.summary: Reardon argues that despite the efforts of struggling men with families, an ever-increasing burden drags them down; society is indifferent to human worth and offers no mercy to those without marketable skills; he accepts some personal responsibility but indicts the system as cruel and blind.
c15:p93.best_quote: The world has no pity on a man who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn't take pity on you you will starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate.
